outline.chapter_title: Introduction: The Challenge of Controlling Diffusion Models
outline.description: This chapter sets the stage by introducing the capabilities of modern text-to-image diffusion models and the specific challenges associated with adapting them for downstream tasks. It defines the two primary tasks addressed in the paper: subject-driven generation and controllable generation. It critiques existing finetuning methods and motivates the need for a new approach based on preserving semantic structure.
subtopics: The Rise of Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
Downstream Tasks: Subject-Driven Generation vs. Controllable Generation
Desiderata for Finetuning: Efficiency and Generalizability Preservation
Limitations of Existing Methods: The Euclidean Distance Fallacy
Introduction to Orthogonal Finetuning (OFT): A Principled Approach

outline.chapter_title: Theoretical Foundations: Neurons and Hyperspherical Energy
outline.description: This chapter provides the necessary theoretical background for understanding OFT. It explores the geometry of neural networks, specifically focusing on the representation of neurons on a unit hypersphere. It introduces the concept of Hyperspherical Energy (HE) as a measure of neuron relationships and explains why preserving this energy is crucial for maintaining the semantic capabilities of pretrained models.
subtopics: Neurons on the Hypersphere: Directions vs. Magnitudes
The Semantic Importance of Angular Information
Defining Hyperspherical Energy (HE)
Hyperspherical Energy as a Measure of Semantic Preservation
How Orthogonal Transformations Preserve Hyperspherical Energy

outline.description: This chapter details the core methodology of the Orthogonal Finetuning framework. It explains the mathematical formulation of applying a layer-shared orthogonal transformation to the weights of a pretrained model. It also addresses the practical challenges of implementing orthogonal constraints efficiently, introducing the Cayley Transform and block-diagonal parameterization.
subtopics: The OFT Framework: Multiplicative Orthogonal Transformation
Mathematical Formulation: Minimizing the Difference in Hyperspherical Energy
Initialization Strategy: Starting from the Pretrained Weights
Efficient Orthogonal Parameterization: The Cayley Transform
Parameter Efficiency: Block-Diagonal Structure
Complexity Analysis: OFT vs. LoRA

outline.chapter_title: Enhancing Stability: Constrained and Re-scaled OFT
outline.description: This chapter explores variations of the base OFT method designed to improve stability and flexibility. It introduces Constrained Orthogonal Finetuning (COFT), which adds an explicit radius constraint to limit the deviation from the pretrained model. It also discusses Re-scaled OFT, which allows for learning magnitude scaling alongside the orthogonal transformation.
subtopics: The Need for Stability: Balancing Flexibility and Regularity
Constrained Orthogonal Finetuning (COFT): The Radius Constraint
Implementing the Constraint: Projected Gradient Descent via Neumann Series
Re-scaled OFT: Learning Magnitude Scaling Coefficients
Analyzing the Trade-off between Flexibility and Regularity

outline.description: This chapter presents the empirical validation of the OFT framework. It details the experimental setup for both subject-driven generation and controllable generation tasks. It analyzes the results in terms of convergence speed, generation quality, and finetuning stability, comparing OFT against baselines like DreamBooth, LoRA, and ControlNet.
subtopics: Task 1: Subject-Driven Generation (DreamBooth Setting)
Evaluation Metrics: Subject Fidelity (DINO, CLIP-I) and Text Alignment
Task 2: Controllable Generation (ControlNet Setting)
A Novel Metric: Control Consistency for Evaluating Controllability
Quantitative Results: Performance over Baselines
Qualitative Analysis: Visualizing Stability and Convergence

outline.description: The final chapter discusses the broader implications of the findings. It provides deeper insights into why OFT works effectively, including its connection to Fourier transforms and optimization landscapes. It addresses practical benefits like the lack of inference overhead and concludes with open problems regarding scalability and compositionality.
subtopics: Why OFT Converges Faster: Optimization Landscapes and Semantic Modifications
Connection to Fourier Transforms: Phase Spectrum and Semantics
Architecture Agnosticism: Applying OFT to Transformers and CNNs
Deployment Efficiency: Zero Additional Inference Overhead
Limitations: Scalability of Matrix Inversion
Future Directions: Compositionality of Orthogonal Matrices
